output.title: Decreasing students’ stress through time management training

scenes.narration: University students often feel stressed, and this paper asks whether a short time management training can change that in higher education.
scenes.layout_description: A student sits at a desk surrounded by papers, with a small clock and stress marks around them.
scenes.visual_prompt: Minimal hand-drawn student at cluttered desk, clock nearby, orange arrows pointing from messy papers toward a simple training booklet, cream background, black ink line art with orange and yellow highlights.

scenes.narration: The authors studied twenty-three undergraduate students who attended one training and reported demands, perceived stress, and perceived control of time before and after.
scenes.layout_description: Three simple icons show the same students at three moments along a timeline.
scenes.visual_prompt: A horizontal timeline with three small student figures at pretest, 2 weeks, and 4 weeks, each beside icons for demands, tension, and control, minimalist line art with highlighted arrows.

scenes.narration: They used a non-equivalent dependent variable design, meaning one outcome should change with training while another similar one should stay unchanged.
scenes.layout_description: Two parallel paths show one variable changing and one staying flat.
scenes.visual_prompt: Split-path diagram: one line rises and one stays level, with a training icon in the middle and a control box labeled by simple hand lettering, orange emphasis on the changing path.

scenes.narration: The training was meant to increase perceived control of time and reduce perceived stress, while demands served as the control variable.
scenes.layout_description: Three labeled circles sit in a balanced row, with the middle two highlighted.
scenes.visual_prompt: Three circles connected to a training booklet: perceived control of time and stress highlighted in yellow/orange, demands shown as a neutral side circle, clean sketch style.

scenes.narration: The intervention focused on prioritizing, goal setting, strategy development, daily planning, and monitoring, all presented as time management strategies.
scenes.layout_description: Five small icons form a simple sequence around a central clock.
scenes.visual_prompt: A clock surrounded by five tiny hand-drawn icons: list, target, steps, calendar, checkmark, with orange arrows showing flow.

scenes.narration: Students first reflected on their activities, then set concrete goals, planned steps, and finally monitored what they had completed each day.
scenes.layout_description: A left-to-right storyboard shows reflection, planning, and checking off tasks.
scenes.visual_prompt: Three-panel sketch of a student thinking, writing goals, and ticking a checklist, with sparse orange highlights on the checklist marks.

scenes.narration: The sample came from a medium-sized German university, and students from all faculties were invited as an extracurricular activity.
scenes.layout_description: A simple campus building with students entering from different directions.
scenes.visual_prompt: Minimal university building, several students carrying books toward a small training room sign, cream background, black line art, orange accent on the sign.

scenes.narration: The training lasted four hours, and questionnaires were completed directly before training, then 2 weeks later, and again 4 weeks later.
scenes.layout_description: A timeline with three survey sheets marks the measurement points.
scenes.visual_prompt: A clean timeline with a clock labeled 4 h and three paper sheets at the measurement points, orange circles around the two follow-up dates.

scenes.narration: Of the forty-eight students, twenty-three completed all questionnaires, and about half of them were female, with a mean age of 23.30 years.
scenes.layout_description: A group of students narrows down to the final twenty-three beside a small age note.
scenes.visual_prompt: A crowd of student figures shrinking to a smaller final group, with a simple age tag and a half-female icon balance, minimalist line art.

scenes.narration: Most participants reported no or little experience with time management strategies before training, which the authors later discuss as important.
scenes.layout_description: A small bar-like cluster shows experience levels, with the first two bars emphasized.
scenes.visual_prompt: Simple hand-drawn experience ladder or bars, with no experience and little experience highlighted in orange, the rest faintly outlined.

scenes.narration: Time management behaviour was measured with eighteen items, perceived stress with the tension scale, perceived control of time with ten items, and demands with five items.
scenes.layout_description: Four measurement cards are arranged in a neat grid with different item counts.
scenes.visual_prompt: Four cards with tiny checklist marks and numbers, one card labeled tension, one control of time, one demands, one time management behaviour, all in minimalist ink.

scenes.narration: The tension scale captured mental fatigue, trouble relaxing, and nervousness, while demands asked about work and external duties.
scenes.layout_description: Two side-by-side panels contrast internal stress reactions and external demands.
scenes.visual_prompt: Left panel shows a tired face and nervous lines; right panel shows stacked tasks and duties, with orange arrows linking them to the questionnaire.

scenes.narration: At time one, time management behaviour correlated positively with perceived control of time, and perceived control of time correlated negatively with stress and demands.
scenes.layout_description: A simple correlation web connects four variables with plus and minus marks.
scenes.visual_prompt: Minimal network diagram with four nodes and thin lines, plus and minus symbols hand-drawn in orange near the relevant links.

scenes.narration: After training, reported use of the taught strategies increased significantly by 4 weeks, and there was a nearly significant increase after 2 weeks.
scenes.layout_description: An upward arrow rises across two follow-up points, with the later point emphasized.
scenes.visual_prompt: A rising line or staircase from baseline to 2 weeks and 4 weeks, with a checkmark at the top and a small question mark at the middle point.

scenes.narration: For perceived stress, the repeated-measures analysis showed a significant overall time effect and a significant effect at 2 weeks after training.
scenes.layout_description: A stress thermometer or wave drops from pretest to the first follow-up.
scenes.visual_prompt: A simple stress gauge with the needle moving downward from pretest to 2 weeks, orange highlight around the lower reading.

scenes.narration: Perceived control of time showed only a tendency at 2 weeks, but by 4 weeks it had increased significantly compared with before training.
scenes.layout_description: A delayed upward curve reaches a clear higher point at the final measurement.
scenes.visual_prompt: A line graph with a modest rise at 2 weeks and a stronger rise at 4 weeks, highlighted with yellow at the final point.

scenes.narration: At 4 weeks, the overall time effect was significant for both outcomes, and students reported less stress and more perceived control of time.
scenes.layout_description: Two outcome icons sit side by side, one falling and one rising.
scenes.visual_prompt: Split illustration: a descending stress cloud on one side and an ascending clock-control icon on the other, both linked to the training booklet.

scenes.narration: The control variable, demands, did not change significantly at either follow-up, which matched the study design.
scenes.layout_description: A flat line for demands runs straight across the timeline.
scenes.visual_prompt: A steady horizontal line labeled demands across three time points, with the training icon nearby but no movement in the line.

scenes.narration: The authors say the pattern supports the conclusion that training reduced perceived stress and increased perceived control of time.
scenes.layout_description: A conclusion box gathers the changing and unchanged lines into one summary arrow.
scenes.visual_prompt: A central summary arrow pointing from training to two outcome icons, with a neutral demands icon off to the side, minimalist and balanced.

scenes.narration: They also note that the effects seemed stronger for students with no or little experience than for those with more experience.
scenes.layout_description: Two small groups are compared, with the less experienced group highlighted more strongly.
scenes.visual_prompt: Two student groups side by side, the less experienced group surrounded by larger orange circles and arrows, the more experienced group with smaller marks.

scenes.narration: The discussion offers possible explanations: better orientation, clearer goals, daily planning, and monitoring may help reduce stress and support control.
scenes.layout_description: Four small icons orbit a student, suggesting practical support.
scenes.visual_prompt: A student in the center with four surrounding icons—goal target, calendar, checklist, and path arrows—linked by orange lines.

scenes.narration: The authors emphasize that the design helped rule out testing, history, and placebo effects better than a simple pretest-posttest study.
scenes.layout_description: A shield-like shape stands between the training and outside threats.
scenes.visual_prompt: A shield around the outcome measures, with small labeled arrows for testing, history, and placebo bouncing away, black ink with orange accents.

scenes.narration: Still, they say a control group or pseudotraining group would be a methodological improvement for future studies.
scenes.layout_description: Two study paths are shown, one with a comparison group and one without.
scenes.visual_prompt: A simple forked study diagram: one path with a second group icon beside it, the other without, with orange arrow pointing to the stronger design.

scenes.narration: The authors describe the study as preliminary because the sample was small and about half the students dropped out before the second measurement.
scenes.layout_description: A small sample icon and a fading participant line show the limited size.
scenes.visual_prompt: A row of student figures with several fading away toward later time points, and a small note-like icon for preliminary, minimalist line art.

scenes.narration: They suggest that future research should compare time management training with other stress-reduction interventions and test whether effects last longer.
scenes.layout_description: Several intervention boxes are arranged around a long timeline.
scenes.visual_prompt: A long timeline with different intervention cards—training, support, exercise, relaxation, meditation—drawn as simple icons, with one orange arrow extending farther right.

scenes.narration: The paper closes by suggesting practical advice for students: prioritize tasks, set clear goals, plan the day, and monitor progress.
scenes.layout_description: A final checklist fills the center of the slide with a calm student beside it.
scenes.visual_prompt: A neat checklist with four simple items and a student giving a thumbs-up, orange checkmarks and a small clock nearby.

scenes.narration: Overall, the study suggests that a short time management training may help undergraduate students feel less stressed and more in control of time.
scenes.layout_description: The closing image combines the clock, checklist, and student into one calm scene.
scenes.visual_prompt: A peaceful student standing beside a clock and completed checklist, with soft orange and yellow highlights indicating reduced stress and improved control, minimalist cream background.
